advisor.summary: A written §127 educational assistance program pays up to $5,250 per employee per year for tuition, fees, books, and supplies — excluded from income and FICA, deductible to the business, with no requirement that the education relate to the job. The exclusion also reaches principal and interest on the employee's qualified education loans, a feature OBBBA made permanent while indexing the cap after 2026. The constraint that disciplines owner planning is §127(b)(3): no more than 5% of benefits may go to >5% owners, their spouses, and their dependents — so the clean family play is a bona fide employed adult child who is neither a dependent nor an equity holder. The engine caps the deduction at $5,250 per participating employee and deducts it at the entity.
mechanics: The §127(b) program requirements: a separate written plan for the exclusive benefit of employees, reasonable notice, no choice between assistance and other taxable compensation, and the 5% concentration limit on the owner class.
Covered benefits span tuition, fees, books, and supplies at any level, job-related or not; meals, lodging, transportation, tools the employee keeps, and most hobby courses do not qualify.
Principal and interest payments on the employee's qualified education loans count toward the same cap — made permanent by P.L. 119-21 (OBBBA), which also indexes the $5,250 for years after 2026.
Excluded amounts are not FICA wages under §3121(a)(18), so employer and employee alike save payroll tax relative to equivalent salary.

The owner-class fence of §127(b)(3): >5% owners, their spouses, and their dependents may not take more than 5% of total benefits — a solo owner cannot self-fund a degree, and a dependent college-age child on payroll sits inside the fence.

Job-related education above the cap can still ride as a §132(d) working-condition fringe grounded in §162 principles — no dollar limit but a strict relatedness standard; and employer-paid loan interest bars the employee's own §221 deduction for the same dollars.

authority.note: The exclusion: the per-employee cap, the written-plan and notice requirements, and loan payments as covered educational assistance.
The owner limitation: >5% owners, their spouses, and their dependents may receive no more than 5% of benefits paid.
Made the student-loan-payment feature permanent and set the $5,250 cap to index for years after 2026.
Keeps §127 amounts out of FICA wages — the payroll-tax layer of the benefit.
The uncapped working-condition-fringe fallback for strictly job-related education beyond the §127 limit.
The deduction standard supporting both the program cost and the §132(d) fallback.
No student-loan interest deduction for interest the employer paid under §127 — the double benefit is closed.

requirements: A separate written plan adopted before benefits are paid, with reasonable notice to employees.
Per-employee benefits held to the cap ($5,250 for 2026; indexed after) — any excess is W-2 wages.
A year-end 5% concentration test across everything paid to the owner class.
For family use: the employed child is bona fide, non-dependent, and holds no equity after attribution.
risks: The concentration test is fractional, and that is the leading exam theory: if the plan's only user sits inside the owner class, 100% of benefits went to restricted persons and the exclusion fails — §127(b)(3) itself is the controlling authority, and no ruling rescues a solo owner's self-funded degree.
A still-dependent child on payroll falls inside the restricted class; the popular pitch of running a dependent's tuition through the business fails on the statute's face.
Bona fide employment of the child is the companion issue — genuine duties, reasonable wages, payroll filings — the same substance discipline as any family-payroll strategy.
Amounts above the cap are wages unless independently excludable as §132(d) job-related education.
stateNotes: Conformity: most federal-AGI states conform to the §127 exclusion, including the loan-payment feature; check any state that decoupled from the loan-payment expansion before promising state-level exclusion.
PTET: the entity's deduction shrinks the pass-through income base on which a PTET election is computed — sequenced, not stacked.

Missouri: conforms on a rolling basis through RSMo §143.121; excluded §127 benefits stay out of Missouri AGI, and a PTET-electing Missouri entity (RSMo §143.436) computes that tax after this deduction.
reviewChecklist: Written plan executed before the first payment; notice to eligible employees documented.
Recipient analysis complete: dependency status and equity (with attribution) verified for every family member.
Per-employee benefits tracked against the current-year cap.
Substantiation — registrar bills, loan statements — collected before each payment.

client.teaser: The business can pay for school or student loans — a deduction for it, tax-free money for them.
client.headline: Have the business pay for education, tax-free
plainEnglish: A business can set up a formal education benefit: up to $5,250 per employee, per year, for tuition, books, fees — and student loan payments too. The business deducts it. The employee pays no tax on it. It even skips payroll taxes, which a raise would not.
The honest part: the rules stop owners from steering this to themselves, their spouses, or the kids they claim on their return. So it cannot pay for your own dependent college student.

Where it shines: employees you want to help with school or student debt, and adult children who truly work in your business and are no longer your dependents. For them, the payments are a clean deduction for you and tax-free money for them.
client.analogy: A $5,250 raise gets taxed before it ever reaches the tuition office. This benefit sends the same dollars straight to the school, with no tax toll along the way.
benefits: Up to $5,250 per employee, per year — deductible and tax-free
Covers student loan payments, not just tuition
Skips payroll taxes on both sides, unlike a raise
A standout perk for hiring and keeping good people
